session.why: A practice session is 60 minutes of track time (plan 5.3), and the clock is what runs out, not the laps. A car leaving the pits spends 60% of a lap getting up to speed and 50% of one coming back in, and stands in the garage for 3 minutes between runs.

programmes.why: What each run programme costs (plan 5.3). A long run is the expensive one: 14 laps on a set that comes back ruined, and it is the only way to see how the compounds go on this track. A qualifying simulation is three laps on a fresh soft. Setup work, fuel calibration and a rookie outing run on used rubber.

fuel.why: Fuel carried in each kind of run, in kilograms: a long run simulates a race stint with 60 kg aboard, a qualifying simulation runs light on 12 kg, everything else takes a working 40 kg. Fuel is why practice times are not information (plan 5.13).

setup.why: A car straight off the truck runs 0.5 s a lap away from where it should be (plan 5.3: practice is what turns time and tyres into a car that works). Setup laps close that gap exponentially on a 5-lap scale, so six laps take out about 70% of it. What is left depends on the race engineer: at 70 he gets it down to 0.08 s, every point above or below moves that by 0.002 s. The full nine-parameter setup arrives in M6; this is the one number it will replace.

qualifying.why: Qualifying as the regulations run it: 18, 15 and 12 minutes, five cars out of each of the first two parts. A car leaves the pits with 10 kg aboard, takes 20 s to get out and an out-lap 30% longer than a flying one. The track starts the hour at 75% of its final grip and a fully evolving track is worth 1.2% of a lap by the end — over a minute and a half that is a tenth or two, which is why everyone wants to be last. A car inside 2.5 s of another at a segment loses up to 0.9 s of that segment, and no lap can lose more than 4% to traffic — past that the driver has backed off and will come round again. Teams choose between four moments in the part, and inside the chosen one every car picks its own second over a 100 s spread — nobody wants to leave the pits in a queue, and in life the field strings itself out over a couple of minutes.

scouting.why: Reading a rival (plan 5.13). One observed lap places another team to about half a second — that is what a fuel and mode correction is worth — and the error falls as the square root of the laps seen. A data-analysis department at 60 reads at that quality; each point is worth 0.8%, down to a floor of 40%. A team running heavy to hide reads about 0.45 s slower than it is, and no correction takes that out, because the lap really was that slow. A team whose character likes a gamble hides more often (appetite 0.55 × its risk), carries 25 kg of ballast for it, and gets half as much out of its own running that session.

learning.why: How much a team learns from running (plan 5.3, 5.13). One long-run lap measures the track's degradation factor to about 0.45 (the factor itself is around 1), and the error falls as the square root of the laps, so a 14-lap run lands near 0.12. Fuel per lap is easier and better known beforehand: 0.02 kg from one lap, so a calibration run leaves under 0.01. A data-analysis department at 60 measures at that quality; every point above or below moves the error 0.6%, down to a floor of 45% — a great department cannot invent data that was never collected. Without practice a team goes to the race on a prior of 0.22 on degradation and 0.025 kg a lap on fuel — about 1.5 kg over a race distance, which is exactly the margin a car is fuelled with, so an uncalibrated team can run to the flag but cannot afford to push.
